en: May the pair of feet of the son of Hiraṇyagarbha— the sprout at the crest of the tree of the Vedas, which bestows prosperity most intensely without depending on anything else,
which is intent on stealing the splendor of the lotus, and which bears the burden of being a hundred-edged thunderbolt for cleaving the mountain of obstacles— extend [prosperity] to us.

If high status in this world is achieved through righteousness, and if its authority is established by words other than those composed by humans, and if the state of their manifestation depends upon the Brahmins, then in their absence, where indeed would my prostration fall? (2)

For prose compositions interspersed with verses blended with aesthetic flavor are indeed as pleasing to the heart as a song accompanied by the art of instrumental music; therefore, may my tongue undertake the composition of the *campū* form for the delight of those who follow the path of poets. (3)
How can I now somehow bring satisfaction to the wise with but a fraction of the fame of the preeminent scion of Raghu as sung by Vālmīki?
Does not a man on earth perform the libation for his ancestors with the waters of the Gaṅgā obtained through the efforts of Bhagīratha? (4)
Having heard the speech of Nārada, that Blessed One, the son of Pracetas and the foremost of poets,
attained for his midday observance the holy river Tamasā, which is frequented by great seers and is the destroyer of all darkness.

There, as the Blessed Vālmīki gazed upon one of a pair of *krauñca* birds—pierced by a hunter’s arrow and already struck by the five-arrowed god of love—a certain stream of speech consisting of poetic meter issued forth from his lotus-like mouth, out of compassion for the bound creature:
"O Niṣāda, may you find no firm footing for eternal years, since you have slain one of the *krauñca* pair while it was infatuated with desire. (6)

Thereafter, when the venerable Vālmīki had returned to his own hermitage after completing the duties appropriate for the occasion, the Lotus-born Lord (Brahmā) appeared as if unable to endure the display of eloquence found elsewhere.
His composition shines like a peacock feather that accomplishes the rite of an Indra-jāla illusion through its manifold manifestations. (7)

Thereafter, having been duly honored by the great sage with supreme joy, the Supreme Lord (Brahmā) vanished after saying: "May you, through this Goddess of Speech (Sarasvatī), who has indeed approached you to manifest your own deeds even in the middle world, expound the life of Rāma exactly as it was heard. Then, by the command of the Lotus-born One, the great sage—who showed the path for those whose speech is full of honey—beheld with his western eye the life of Rāma as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand, and composed the auspicious and sweet poem known as the *Rāmāyaṇa*.

While the Blessed Vālmīki was reflecting on who would be capable of performing this composition, there arrived two men named Kuśa and Lava— each resembling the other, both deeply learned, endowed with voices as sweet as the Vedas,
discerning, and possessing the various marks of a sovereign. (9)

The sage, having taken these two under his care, taught them his own composition. Seeing them wandering here and there singing it, Rāma, with a joyful heart, brought them to his palace and, surrounded by his brothers, directed them to sing of his own life-story. Then those two youths, disciples of that preeminent sage—the abode of words composed in meter—began to sing the deeds of the hero of the Raghus in due order. (10)
In the Kosala country, which bestows joy upon the eyes of the people, there exists the praiseworthy city of Ayodhyā, belonging to the Raghus, whose commands have driven away the Dānavas. (11)
Daśaratha dwelt there, sharing his seat with Saṅkrandana, who is praised by the gods;
his dwelling was perfumed by the honey from mandāra garlands obtained in the world of the gods during his victory over the enemies of the immortals.

Then, while Daśaratha—his mind tormented by childlessness—was deliberating with his ministers on how to perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice for the sake of a son, Sumantra, with a joyful heart, recounted to Daśaratha an ancient legend told by Sanatkumāra: that through the grace of the great seer Ṛṣyaśṛṅga—the son of Vibhāṇḍaka, who was renowned for his power to suppress droughts even when encountered in the land of Aṅga—the birth of princes would surely come to pass.

At the words of Sumantra, his mind pacified, he brought the sage Śāntākuṭumbin as a relative; having performed the Aśvamedha sacrifice as instructed by Vasiṣṭha on the banks of the Sarayū, he began to duly perform the Putreṣṭi sacrifice there.

Subsequently, all the hosts of gods led by Indra descended to the earth to fetch the sacrificial offerings. Having informed the Four-faced One (Brahmā) of the scorching heat of the summer of Rāvaṇa’s prowess, they approached the Ocean of Milk along with him, regarding the wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Viṣṇu) as their refuge, while offering various kinds of extemporized hymns of praise.

He beheld the one known as Vaikuṇṭha—the destroyer of the heat of all worlds, beautiful with his Śārṅga bow, shimmering with the lightning of Lakṣmī, his body possessing the hue of a cluster of *atasī* flowers, the refuge for the *cātaka*-birds that are the minds of sages, an ocean of compassion, and a dark cloud to the assembly of the gods. (13)
He who, with the sprouts of light from his body, brings about an identity with the petals of blue lotuses blossoming in due time all around the interior of the milk-ocean;
and who, upon the serpent-couch, assumes a certain sleep-posture as pale as linen, yet remains ever vigilant in the protection of the entire world. (14)

In order to simultaneously shatter the boundless calamity of Prahlāda, the hypocrisy and arrogance of the host of Daityas, and even the chest of his enemy, he assumed the form of a lion with a human body—his fangs blazing in a world brightened by their luster—to swiftly pierce those who were fixed in faith. (15)

Salutations to the Supreme Person, Nārāyaṇa, whose eyes are as long as lotus petals, who reduced the majesty of Mahābali to nothing but a name, and whose nostrils are the source of the creation of the manifold moving and non-moving beings. 16.

Having thus prostrated, the lotus-eyed Lord, gladdening all the immortals headed by Indra—whose faces were resonant with the sound of praise—as they rose up, with streams of light from his eyes that stole the grace of the dawn-red lotus, spoke clearly:
"O immortals, is all well? Welcome to you now; has the sport of the thunderbolt ceased its deception of the demons?
Do the paths of policy fashioned by the intellect of Bṛhaspati suffice for the task of securing the welfare of the city of the thirty gods? (17)

Having thus heard the Lord’s speech, which was preceded by his application to virtue and was as flavorful as a shower of nectar, the assembly of gods—their desires fully realized—addressed the Supreme Person: "O Lord! How could any misfortune befall us who have found refuge in you? Nevertheless, there exists a royal capital of the night-stalkers named Laṅkā, which cannot be bypassed even by the gods of exalted power."
With the sprouts of light from the floors of her ruby palaces, she displays the state of a lamp for the day to the threefold brilliance [of the sun, fire, and moon]. ||18||

In this ancient city, which is as magnificent as the city of the gods, the king named Rāvaṇa—whose arms are as delightful as the *sāla* trees, who has conquered the king of the Yakṣas, and who effortlessly overcomes the night-stalkers of the world—protects it for a long time. (19)

Those whose arms act as the edge of a sword and swallow the moon of the fame of the world-protectors—there is no one at all who can grant refuge to their enemies on the front lines of battle except for this Death. (20)
By propitiating this lotus-born one with many austerities, he obtained a boon difficult for others to attain; from that [boon],
the entire world [fell] under his own command.
The sovereign of the night-rangers makes him his target. ||21||
Because of this, we have become as if dependent upon another.
For instance,

should he ever ascend a mountain peak for sport accompanied by the women of his harem and traverse it on foot, the divine thousand-rayed sun, fearing that its heat might be revealed, would surely shrink its beams out of dread and take refuge upon those very ridges.

This Mṛgāṅka, too, in order to rest from the exhaustion of the hunt, hurriedly approached the bathing chamber where the Ten-faced one was surrounded by his attendants as he prepared to bathe. There, he caused a stream of water—pure and falling in an unbroken flow—to issue from the mouth of a crystal jar held in the palm of a stone statue carved upon the top of a most exquisite golden pillar; by the touch of his own hand, he became for a moment the recipient of those twenty kinds of glances, long desired by Śunāsīra (Indra), which were indicative of his favor.

Because the basin of that tree has its soil saturated by the lukewarm water trickling from the golden jars held in the lotus-hands of Pulastya’s son—who brought the host of celestial trees, headed by the Mandāra, from Indra’s pleasure garden—and from the pair of blue-lotus eyes of the captive celestial beauties, the winds are not even able to stir; fearing the fall of their blossoms, they remain apprehensive even of those flowers that have already reached full maturity.
These fires as well, bearing the name "fire" (hutavaha) which evokes the suspicion of being a common fire, yet preceded by the Gārhapatya fire, assume the role of a chief cook in that house.

"What more need be said? Thinking that he would suffer no insult from a mere mortal, and having obtained invulnerability from others through a boon from the Four-Faced One (Brahmā), Rāvaṇa has now become arrogant. With his chest scarred by the indentations of wounds inflicted by the spear-like tusks of elephants that traverse the horizons in battle, he oppresses the three worlds like a wild elephant trampling a lotus-pond; thus, he knows nothing at all of us who belong to you.
Then the Blessed One, hearing the speech of the host of gods, smiled with a radiance as white as moonlight rising upon a mountain of sapphire.
Madhusūdana spoke words that were sweet like a stream of nectar.
"It is possible for you to bring about the immediate destruction of that Yātudhāna who has committed this offense against you;

however, honoring even the command of the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā) and fulfilling the desire of Daśaratha—who, though a friend of Sutrāman (Indra), regards the earth as his own daughter—I shall slay him myself, assuming a human guise. Having spoken thus, he vanished.

Then that assembly of gods, their joy blossoming with wide-open eyes, departed from the Ocean of Milk after learning that the fourteen worlds, including the ten-headed Rāvaṇa, had been delivered from calamity by the command of Hṛṣīkeśa (Viṣṇu).

Then the Grandfather spoke to those immortals: "In order to provide assistance to Lakṣmī’s consort as he descends, you shall procreate offspring of renowned power among young women such as Apsarases, assuming the forms of monkeys, bears, gopucchas, and blue-faced apes.
Indeed, it is said that at the very beginning of my yawning, Jāmbavān was born."
Then those gods did accordingly.

Then, from the Vaiśvānara fire of the sacrifice, a certain man belonging to the lineage of Prajāpati rose up, holding a golden vessel; he offered milk-rice (*pāyasa*), which was like nectar, to Daśaratha, who was desiring a son.
The king first assigned half of that milk-rice to Kausalyā.
He gave half [of himself] to the daughter of the King of Kekaya, sweet with affection;
these two queens, perceiving the state of mind of their fickle-minded husband, themselves made Sumitrā one whose desires were fulfilled by means of their own respective halves.
When the final ablution was completed and the people had departed from the banks of the Sarayū each to their own homes,
Daśaratha, his desires fully realized, returned to the city which resembled the city of Indra.

Due to the slight indisposition of their limbs alone, the signs of pregnancy belonging to the queens— whose lovely splendor remained unimpaired— gradually shone forth as they cast off their ornaments.

With her three folds of skin slowly receding and the cave of her navel becoming a realm of profound depth, the slender waist of the daughter of the Lord of Kosala also gradually came within the range of vision. (26)
The belly of the slender-limbed lady again assumed the likeness of a banyan leaf, as it gradually grew,
for the sake of the life of those tormented by the ten-headed serpent.
By the first Puruṣa dwelling under the guise of an embryo. ||27||
The waist of that dark-eyed maiden was so slender as to be imperceptible; at the time of her conception, it had become like space itself under the guise of Viṣṇu’s footstep.
Having abandoned even emaciation, one has indeed abandoned it. ||28||
When five planets were situated in exaltation, Jupiter was with the Moon, on the ninth lunar day (navamī),
in the Cancer ascendant conjoined with the Punarvasu nakṣatra, and the Sun had entered Aries; then,
from the sacrificial fire-pit of Ayodhyā, all the palāśa fuel-sticks were consumed as if by a forest fire.
Another singular, unprecedented majesty has become manifest. ||29||
Then, perfuming the speech of the poet named Rāma, Hari, out of compassion, graced the lineage of the Raghus. (30)
Nevertheless, three others were born after him, possessing the brilliance of the three sacred fires,
emulating their elder brother through those various superhuman qualities.
Among them, Bharata was the son of Kaikeyī, resplendent with discipline;
the other two, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna, were born of Sumitrā.
These heroes grew up, consecrated for the protection of the sacred word (brahma), like the four arms of Mukunda, the source of joy to the worlds. ||33||

Then, on one occasion, King Daśaratha—his chariot surrounded by a host of gods who were fleeing in all directions after being attacked by the army of the Daityas, which was formidable with its immeasurable power of illusion—beheld the venerable son of Kuśika, the performer of the sacrifice for Triśaṅku; he was a repository of wonders born of ascetic practice, appearing like a poetic composition in which the divisions of creation are displayed, or like a Prakrit grammar in which the transposition of phonemes is made manifest, or like Budha, the son of Soma.

Thereafter, the son of Gadhin (Vasiṣṭha), who had performed his worship according to the rules, whose greatness transcended all bounds, who was honored by all, and whose heart was unfathomable, was thus entreated by the king for the sake of protecting the sacrifice:

"O King, having completed the protection of the sacrifice—which is being performed by your son Rāma, who is delightful in his discipline, who has the bow as his friend, and whose only retinue is the son of Sumitrā—I desire to cross over the calamity caused by the Rākṣasas and perform the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
Upon hearing these words of the great sage, which were harsh to the ear, the husband of Kausalyā felt his heart pierced by arrows due to his excessive affection for his son.

Then, while the blessed Viśvāmitra remained firm in his resolve despite many attempts to dissuade him, Daśaratha was thus addressed by his family priest, who acted for the welfare of the solar dynasty:
"You should offer hospitality to this son of Kuśika, whose fortune is fully merited;
let Rāma go forth with Lakṣmaṇa to rid the earth of the Yātudhānas. (34)

Thus, Daśaratha, his resolve firmly established by Vasiṣṭha, fulfilled the desire of the son of Kuśika by the gift of his sons. This very Rāma, who is attainable through yoga by men whose minds are detached from worldly existence, followed after Kauśika at the command of his father. (35)
There, in order to protect the sacrifice, the great sage Viśvāmitra,
leading Rāma along with the son of Sumitrā, spoke as follows:
"O descendant of Kakutstha, the two sciences known as Balā and Atibalā, which were obtained by me through the power of my austerities, exist within me; I bestow them upon you."
Then, having shown a certain region to the son of Daśaratha who had mastered the sciences, the Blessed One spoke thus:
"In this place, in former times, when the fire of the eye from between the brows of the Supreme Lord, the Destroyer of Cities, blazed forth, the Mind-born [God of Love]..."
Immediately assuming the state of a moth, it abandoned its body there;
therefore, O Vidura, that region is known by the name Aṅga.

Thereafter, having crossed the Sarayū river flowing from Lake Mānasa, as the two sons of Daśaratha set foot upon the border of the two districts named Malada and Karūṣa—which had acquired their purity by washing away the mire of Indra’s sin incurred during the slaying of Vṛtra—the Yakṣa spoke again as follows:
“By the grace of Brahmā, Suketu obtained a certain daughter named Tāṭakā.
It is said that Sunda married her and begot upon her the base Mārīca. (39)

Once, when Sunda had been slain, Mārīca, having overwhelmed the Pot-born Sage (Agastya), fell under his curse and became a demon; Tāṭakā likewise became a devourer of men. She, possessing the strength of a thousand elephants perfected by the Lotus-seated One (Brahmā), was causing calamity to the countryside and must be killed by you along with her son. Upon hearing this, Rāma felt apprehension regarding the killing of a woman.

Furthermore, by showing him Vairocanī (Mandodarī), who was slow-witted, who bore the burden of offenses against the Earth, and who had been slain by Purandara; and by showing him the mother of Bhārgava (Kauśikī), who had been crushed by Janārdana, he dispelled the prince’s intense hesitation regarding the slaughter of Sundā’s wife.
Having heard from him of the slaying of Sundā’s beloved through his learned conduct, his bow spoke the very same thing to him under the guise of its twanging sound.
At that moment, a certain fierce ogress named Tāṭakā, who was as hideous as twilight and as cruel as flesh-eating demons, violently blocked the sage’s path;

she was dreadful, stained with blood and gore, and while death was already within her power, she made the city’s central crossroads a place of peril for the throngs of Yama’s servants who were sporting in the failure of their assigned tasks.
Then the virtue of Tāṭakā entered the ear of the son of Daśaratha;
likewise, the string of his bow quickly entered [his mind] with the desire to slay her.
Then, as the battle was about to take place, Tāṭakā, filled with faith in him, offered her own life as a libation for the hero’s drink for Rāma’s arrow. (43)
The Sage gave the weapons, beginning with the Jṛmbhaka, which had been first discovered by Bhṛśāśva, to the slayer of Tāṭakā at the command of the subduer of Jambha.
There, pointing out a certain region that was a reproach to the world of Viriñci, he said:
"In this place, which is daily attended with reverence by pure Brahmins devoted to the Absolute, whose exhaustion from worldly existence has been stilled."
For the purpose of subduing Bali, Vāmana, intent on the restraint of Bali, wandered in this forest as a celibate student (brahmacārī). ||45||

This exceedingly dark row of trees belonging to the hermitage of Vāmana—who, in his unborn form, had removed the afflictions of the gods and who was a mendicant for all the worlds—pervades the boundaries of the quarters and the sky; it seems as if it itself is striving to measure the world.
Thus, as the two sons of Daśaratha proceeded, their profound hardships having dissolved through these purifying stories— uttered by Kauśika, rich in various sentiments, and sweet to the ear.
The length of the road seemed to contract instantly as if it were such [a short distance]. ||47||
Then, having entered Siddhāśrama, Viśvāmitra commenced a sacrificial session (*satra*).

Immediately thereafter, beholding that swarm of *palāśa* trees descending from the midst of the sky—terrifying as the army of Death—the disciples of the son of Kuśika fled in agitation, dropping their fuel and sacred grass (*samit-kuśa*) from their hands; they then reported with great haste to Rāghava, who was eager for battle, [the arrival of] those [trees] which, having seized the peaks of the mountain, were casting them about on all sides and laughing in fury.
Clapping their hands here and there, dancing repeatedly,
sprinkling the earth with a garland made of entrails, binding the sky-dwellers by their hair,
and burning the night-stalkers with eyes like fire, they block the gateway to heaven.

As if through the merit of contact with the son of Gadhi, whose complexion had been transferred [to him], Rāmabhadra, though worthy of the staff of Pippala according to the Kṣatriya tradition, held in his hand the Palāśa staff. (49)
Having instigated a battle with a base mind, Mārīca was struck in an instant by the arrow of the Lord of the Raghus;
his body submerged in the midst of the ocean out of fear, he assumed a form indistinguishable from a water-man (jalamānuṣa).
Subāhu, intoxicated by his own prowess, was struck down by the arrow of the descendant of Kakutstha;
unwelcome to the sages, he was made a guest of the Lord of the Dead.
Touched by the bamboo, accompanied by an arrow discharged by Rāma that bore heart-captivating fruit,
and moistened with resin, it emerged as if full of passion.
The life-force of the flesh-eaters departed from their hearts.
Then, the sage, having dispelled the obstacles to his sacrificial rites by means of the night-stalking demons and having completed the heart-pleasing concluding bath (avabhṛtha),
reflected that Rāma had joined him in battle with the goddess of victory.
[He was] joined with the goddess Lakṣmī, whose form was produced by sacrifice, through a union that was not born of water. || 53 ||
Then, having set out toward Mithilā, Kauśika spoke thus to the descendant of Kakutstha:

"In former times, indeed, a royal sage named Kuśa, born from the lotus-seated Brahmā, had four sons—headed by Kuśāmba—who were the founders of the cities known as Kauśāmbī, Mahodaya, Dharmāraṇya, and Girivraja.
Kuśanābha, moreover, begot a hundred daughters upon Ghṛtācī."
Desiring those maidens who were already endowed with youth, Pavamāna, his anger provoked by their rejection, spread wickedness throughout their limbs.

Then, King Kuśanābha, having learned of this occurrence and considering forgiveness alone to be the proper remedy, gave them to Brahmadatta, the son of Cūli and king of the Saumadeyas; thus they returned to their natural state.
Furthermore, desiring sons, Kuśanābha begot through the grace of his father our venerable grandfathers, known as the Gādhis, who possessed unfathomable courage.

Thus the son of Daśaratha, having spent the watches of the night without weariness by listening to the account of Kauśika’s birth, set out along the path leading to the Gaṅgā—by which path he was accompanied by the sage who had performed his morning rites and observed his vows—as the eastern quarter was turned crimson by the twilight glow, as beautiful as a cluster of Bandhūka flowers, bearing the name Śoṇa because of that river.
He reached that river, which is like the Earth (Gā): pure with its milk-like waters born of the soil, bestowing joy upon the bulls [or: the virtuous], and beloved by the Vedas [or: the ears]. (54)
Then the Blessed One spoke this to Rāma, who was desirous of hearing the story of Bhāgīrathī:
"In ancient times, there was a daughter of Sumeru named Manoramā;
by her alone did the mountain-king become a householder and a sovereign emperor."
She had two daughters; one of them was Mandākinī, and the other was the goddess herself, the wife of the Moon-crested Lord.
Having obtained that river, the gods led her to the world of heaven;
meanwhile, the Mountain gave Gaurī, who was performing ascetic penance, to the Great God.
Seeing that the seed of Śiva and Pārvatī had been deposited in the womb,
Pāvaka (the Fire-god), entreated by the deities, received it.
The wrath of Ambikā, arising from her failure to obtain a son, rendered the earth childless, helpless, and immortal, yet possessed of many wives. (59)
Then, urged by the gods together with Brahmā who desired a commander-in-chief,
Agni immediately cast the seed of Īśvara into the Jāhnavī.
She too, unable to bear that splendor cast by the seven-rayed fire,
being exhausted, abandoned it in a forest of reeds in the wilderness on the slopes of the Himalayas.
There, for the sake of pleasing Kṛttikā, there appeared the splendor of the six-faced one (Kārttikeya), whose lotus-face was mounted upon six [peacocks],
which instantly destroyed the darkness of the stars.
"Listen, my child, to the threefold nature of the river of the gods, which consumes the oblation just as a deity does at a sacrifice. (53)
King Sagara, the son of Sāvitra, who had completed his first stage of life (brahmacarya), resided in the city of Ayodhyā together with Keśinī and Sumati.
Desiring a son, he performed austerities together with his wife for a hundred years;
Bhṛgu, being pleased in mind, bestowed upon him the wealth of an heir.
Keśinī, the daughter of Vidarbha, bore Asamañjas as their son; and Sumati, the younger of the two, bore sixty thousand sons.
Having cast off his improper conduct and his impropriety, he,
having commenced the horse sacrifice, released the steed.
This horse was carried off by Hari in the form of a flesh-eating demon;
thereupon, the sons of Sumati set out to search for him who had vanished.
Digging up the entire earth along with its mountains, all the sons of Sagara made the world of the Nagas appear as if its darkness were shattered by the rays of their nails.
These heroes, in that blazing fire of Kapila which was kindled by ascetic power and which destroys the mass of darkness, met their end like moths.
Then he spoke to Aṃśumat, the grandson of Asamañja:
"Having taken the horse, may you complete the sevenfold sacrifice. (71)
He too, having gone there to the cave and seeing his ancestors reduced to ashes, offered a salutation with joined palms while shedding tears; he then obtained the horse from them.
Their maternal uncle Garuḍa spoke thus to him right there:
"O long-lived one, bring the Gaṅgā here; she is their supreme refuge."
Then, having heard the news of his son and having recovered the horse,
Sagara concluded the sacrifice and ascended to heaven out of grief for his son.
Then Aṃśumān, having protected the kingdom for a long time,
performed ascetic penance on the Himalayas after entrusting the burden of the earth to Dilīpa.
When Dilīpa had also gone to heaven, Bhagīratha, having heard the news,
resolved to transform the river of mortals into the river of the immortals.
Then, while Bhagīratha was performing austerities at Gokarṇa,
the Lord, a treasure-house of compassion, consented to carry the celestial river.
Then, the expanse of the sky and the quarters of space were covered by a mass of waves;
it was jagged with the pearls of stars interspersed among the conchs of the moon.
The eastern quarter had its Aruṇa (the Dawn) distressed by the sun-horses drawn along by the waves;
and Vāsava (Indra) was preoccupied with arrows aimed at his own elephant, which was covered in foam. 79.
With its branches and crest-tips revealed, it uprooted the trees of the Nandana grove;
there, the sun was bewildered regarding the directions, the path of the sky, and the single expanse of water.
The river was a calamity for the floating celestial chariots, which were bewildered by its whirlpools and deep eddies;
its green banks were adorned with streaks of dark clouds that resembled moss.
The river of the world of the gods, overwhelmed by the weight of its own pride,
fell into the deep thicket of the matted locks of Pārvatī’s beloved.
Finding no exit from Śambhu’s matted locks, the celestial river assumed the likeness of a drop of frost clinging to the tip of a blade of dūrvā grass.
Not seeing that river there, Bhagīratha, his desires frustrated by the cruelty of Brahmā, praised the Supreme Lord.
The Gaṅgā, having assumed seven forms, descended upon the summit of the mountain;
being pleased by that hymn of praise, she was cast by him into the Bindu-saras lake.
Among them, three flowed toward the east, heading toward the eastern quarter;
another followed the path of Bhagīratha, who was intent on performing ancestral rites.
This very Bhāgīrathī river surrounded the sacrificial ground of Jahnu;
having drunk her up, he then became pacified and released her through the path of his ear.
By means of that river, the Jāhnavī, Bhagīratha caused his ancestors to reach heaven; with his desires fully realized, he returned to his own city.
Then the son of Daśaratha, having heard the account of the Bhāgīrathī and having crossed that river, beheld a vast city and asked Gādhi’s son, "To whom does this belong?
He replied as follows:

"Long ago, indeed, when a mutual conflict arose between the gods and the demons for the sake of the nectar (*sudhā*), Viśvarūpa displayed his world-deluding illusion (*māyā*) and caused the destruction of the Daityas by means of the hand [of Indra] wielding the hundred-edged thunderbolt."

Their mother, Diti, filled with excessive wrath and desiring to obtain some son who would govern Śatamanyu (Indra), performed penance for a very long time at Kuśaplava at the word of her husband Mārīca. While she was serving him with feigned devotion, the wielder of the hundred-edged thunderbolt (Indra), perceiving that she had fallen asleep with the mass of her hair caught under his foot, deemed her impure and entered her womb. He emerged after splitting the embryo into seven parts. Diti, having learned of the fate of her sons, caused even those fragments to be made into the Seven Maruts by Ākhaṇḍala (Indra) and entered heaven.
Then, a certain lord of the earth was born to Alambusā from Ikṣvāku;
he founded here the city named Viśālā after his own name. (89)

Thereafter, having been received as a guest by the king named Sumati who resided there, the venerable Viśvāmitra, accompanied by the prince, spent the night there and set out toward Mithilā. Having shown him the hermitage of Gautama, the most eminent of ascetics, he related this story concerning that sage’s wife: "Mahendra came here by a path frequented by the ignoble, approaching the lawful wife of Gautama.
Enraged, the sage rendered the bull [Indra] seedless and made his wife invisible. (90)
"When Rāma has gone to this forest, you shall be released from the curse.
Having spoken thus to his wife, Gautama departed for the Himalayas to perform austerities.
When the host of deities had thus learned the account,
the Bull (Śiva) obtained the testicles of the Ram through the power of the Pitṛs.
"Therefore, let Gautama accept her as one freed from sin.
Thus, accompanied by Rāma, Kauśika entered his hermitage.
In that great matter concerning both the suffering and the joy of Gautama’s lawful wife, passion alone was the cause;
for she had undergone a transformation through the quality of *rajas*.
By the dust of Rāma’s feet, she returned to her natural state. || 94 ||

Having accepted the hospitality extended by Gautama and Ahalyā, Viśvāmitra, accompanied by the princes, took up residence in Janaka’s sacrificial pavilion on the land near Mithilā. Thereafter, when he had been duly honored by Janaka, Śatānanda, the family priest of the Ikṣvāku lineage, addressed the descendant of Raghu as follows: "Standing in the conduct appropriate for a Kṣatriya, this sage went to the hermitage of the son of Brahmā; having received hospitality there, he learned that [the cow] Surabhi’s power was boundless."

She was solicited by him; when that best of sages did not consent, she dragged him away while crying out, and by her alone, who possessed such great power, he became utterly terrified and fled in all directions. || 95 ||

The husband of Arundhatī stood firm, obstructing with the Brahmadaṇḍa the succession of divine weapons of that king—who was repeatedly terrified by his power, who had acquired various weapons through the force of asceticism, and who had again commenced battle for the sake of the Surabhi cow—by means of his own supreme weapon.

Thereupon, having become dejected and concluding that the supreme Brahmanic splendor alone is greater than the Kṣatriya luster, he performed most intense penance in the southern direction in order to attain it.

Now, Triśaṅku, a Kṣatriya of the solar lineage, having been rejected by Vasiṣṭha despite his petition for the attainment of heaven in his own body, was cursed to the state of a Caṇḍāla by Vasiṣṭha’s sons—Mahodaya and the others—who were provoked by his persistence. He then sought refuge with him (Viśvāmitra). Viśvāmitra, too, commenced a sacrifice to fulfill his desire. When the Brāhmaṇas had assembled there, out of loathing for Triśaṅku, he cursed Vasiṣṭha’s sons, who had not arrived, making them eaters of dogs.
Then, even while the host of gods had descended from heaven,
this Great-Souled One, by the power of his asceticism, caused Triśaṅku—
clad in blue garments, devoid of royal insignia, and indistinguishable in dress from the midnight of the rainy season— to ascend to heaven.
Filled with wrath, Śatamanyu struck him as he was seeking refuge in heaven;
then, having taken hold of the peg of his sacrificial post, Triśaṅku obtained a firm footing in the sky.

Then, having abandoned his task of creating other worlds at the request of the hosts of gods, he was performing intense penance at Puṣkara in the western direction when an obstacle to his asceticism arose. At that moment, Śunaḥśepa—the middle son of Ṛcīka—having been purchased with many cows as a substitute for a human victim to serve as an expiation for the destruction of sacrificial animals during King Ambarīṣa’s sacrifice, approached him and sought refuge.

This Blessed One, intent on protecting him by exchanging his own son for him, inflicted upon Haviṣyanda and the others—who had turned their faces away—the state of being sons of Vasiṣṭha through a curse; and having been pleased by two verses, he caused Indra and Upendra to fulfill the desires of both Ambarīṣa and Śunaḥśepa.
Then, while he was performing austerities, the interruption of his penance brought about by union with Menakā persisted for a long time.
Later, overcome by remorse, he performed severe austerities on the northern mountain on the banks of the Kauśikī.

There, having cursed Rambhā—who had been sent by Jambhāri—saying "Become a stone," he performs penance in that eastern direction with his breath suppressed. The lotus-seated Brahmā, whose friends are the gods, being distressed by the heat of his ascetic fire, approached him and said, "Since you have conquered your senses, even Vasiṣṭha, the celestial sage, should address you thus.
By the instruction of Vasiṣṭha, he attained the status of a celestial sage, just as one becomes twice-born through the rite of initiation attains spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Thus praised by the priest of Janaka, the son of Gādhi,
having spent the night there with the two princesses,
offered the traditional *arghya* oblation containing flowers and the tips of *darbha* grass according to the prescribed rites.
To the beloved of the lotus, to the light, to the one who knows the Vedic meters. || 99 ||

Thereafter, having entered the capital city of Janaka—its royal highway lined with the radiance of the eyes of the city’s women, which, falling incessantly out of curiosity to behold Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, was darkened by a swarm of blossoming blue lotuses as it stole away their deep black luster—Viśvāmitra addressed the son of Daśaratha as follows:
"In this very city, by the grace of King Janaka who had commenced a sacrifice, the divine Earth, whose womb contains all jewels, gave birth to a jewel among maidens named Sītā.
What more need be said of her greatness?"
The ocean was her garment, Mount Meru her footstool, and the Sindhu river—her sole companion on the path to heaven for the sons of Sagara—was her necklace;
the pleasure-mountain was the tusk of the Boar, the First Person, upon whose lap she rested: it is said that in this world, Mithilā was the birth-chamber of Sītā’s mother. 100.
There, for the sake of Sītā’s marriage— an undertaking difficult even for the gods— Janaka established the stringing of the bow as the condition.
Then the great seer entered King Janaka’s assembly hall, which resembled the Sudharmā council of the gods;
and the two of them arrived, their eyes restless with the desire to behold the bow.
The two princes of Kosala were accompanied by their wives. || 102 ||

There, having been duly honored and informed of the account of Daśaratha’s son, Kauśika directed Rāma to string that bow— which had been entrusted by the gods, headed by Kaśyapa, to Devarāta, the elder of our lineage, and which Janaka had pointed out as being specially preserved by him for the purpose of Sītā’s bride-price.
Then,
while Rāma displayed the strength of his arms, the string was fixed upon the bow.
It was not only the lineage of the son of Vikartana (Karna), adorned by himself,
that was utterly pulled down; for not only was Sita’s heart swiftly broken,
but the pride of the pillar-like arms of the kings was shattered as well.
The sound produced by the breaking of the bow during Rāma’s drawing of it, which filled the space between heaven and earth,
acted like the roar of clouds over the white-winged flocks of the fame of arrogant Kṣatriyas;
at the moment of the Heroic Fortune’s first entrance, it acted like the proclamation of an auspicious day.
Indeed, in Sītā’s heart, it acted as the auspicious musical instrument for her marriage.

The sharp sound, born from the bowstring snapping under the fresh strain of the hard-drawn bow, instantly offered a welcome to the Lord of the Quarters with the trumpeting of the elephants of the cardinal directions;
it spread a loud resonance like the sound of a marching drum for the lady of Rāma’s fame as she set out, rising up in her eagerness to wander through the world.
There, Daśaratha, summoned by a messenger sent by Janaka who had resolved upon Sītā’s marriage, arrived at Mithilā following the acceptance of the priest.

His fame serves as a tilaka-mark at the forefront of the musical assemblies of the celestial damsels; through him the first man became a father of a son, and by him alone the earth became possessed of a true king.
It was Indra who, in the perils of battle, met with misfortune merely from seeing the hem of the garment on the banner of that hero’s chariot as it swayed upward.
Janaka summoned his younger brother Kuśadhvaja,
who had slain Sudhanvan in battle and was established in the city of Sāṅkāśya.
Thereafter, honored by the two of them, Daśaratha, together with his family priest, performed the auspicious *godāna* ceremony for his sons.
By the command of his father, Rāghava accepted Sītā from Janaka, just as the sacrificial fire accepts the oblation from the patron of the sacrifice according to the injunctions of the Vedas. (108)
This is a marvel:
having fixed some quality upon the bow of the Unblinking One, Rāmabhadra accepted Sītā according to the word of the son of Kuśika.
Thereafter, Lakṣmaṇa, his younger brother, who had instilled many virtues in the heart of the Lord of Mithilā, [married] Ūrmilā as well. ||109||
Then, by the command of Kuśadhvaja, Bharata and Śatrughna became householders with Māṇḍavī and Śrutakīrti respectively.

Then Daśaratha, returning from Videha with his sons who had completed their marriages, beheld on the road the sage Paraśurāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu. This son of Bhṛgu was one whose wrath was as unbearable as the fire blazing at the end of an aeon, possessed of terrifying and irresistible prowess, and who had performed the libations for his ancestors with streams of blood drawn by the edge of his axe that stripped away the pride of the entire class of Kṣatriyas. He was the foremost among the arrogant and fierce in majesty; though clad in the bark garments appropriate for asceticism, his zeal for battle had not been entirely extinguished due to the persistence of his latent tendencies.

And upon merely beholding him, though his joy was already diminished, he performed the rites of hospitality along with the great sages and asked, "O noble one, is all well? Then, hearing those gracious words of Daśaratha, the Lord of the Bhṛgus spoke these humble words to Rāmabhadra:
"I had come desiring to humble the pride of the arms of that man whose fame was earned from the old bow, but who remained unaware of your axe—his pride in this [new] bow. (111)
Taking that arrow with its feathers, quickly preparing it,
and fixing it upon the bow, the wise one, feeling compassion for the life of that ascetic, reflected upon his state as a man of penance.
Rāma desisted from the battle that had become truly terrible. ||112||
And both of them, born of the lineage of Bhṛgu and descended from Atri,
Daṇḍa, and Jamadagni,
relied solely upon a humble disposition.
They both became endowed with virtues dedicated to Rāghava. ||113||
When the qualities of straightness and crookedness were simultaneously attained by Cāpa and Bhārgavarāma, straightness acquired crookedness and crookedness likewise acquired straightness. (114)

Then, at that very moment, Rāghava blocked Bhārgava’s path to heaven with an unerring arrow; for it was indeed fitting. Truly, an offense committed against a great man by an ordinary person inevitably yields a fruit corresponding to its gravity.
Having momentarily obstructed the course of the descendant of Raghu, Bhārgava thus incurred a blow from that master of supreme power. ||115||

Then, having embraced Rāma—who was endowed with the power of the son of Jamadagni that had been transferred to him and who was as beautiful as the coils of the lord of serpents—and having smelled the crown of his head, Daśaratha entered Ayodhyā, which was intersected by the Sarayū river flowing around its perimeter like a moat; he entered while the city’s matrons, gazing longingly at their children and their wives, filled the windows with side-glances that surpassed the beauty of peacock feathers, serving as white parasols in place of those made of peacock plumes.
Out of modesty, with their amorous transformations not yet fully manifest, those brides experienced excessive pleasure;
thus the eldest [of the princes], skilled in the union of youth, enjoyed the four primary flavors from the sons of the Lord of the Ikṣvākus.

Through that princess, who possessed an intellect as sharp as the tip of a blade of darbha grass and whose vision was like the three Vedas, Rāma attained supreme joy, as if through sacred knowledge itself. (117)
Thus ends the Bālakāṇḍa in the Campūrāmāyaṇa composed by Vidarbharāja.
Having departed, King Daśaratha, by the strength of his own arms, secured for the kings a state of bliss difficult to attain;
meanwhile, Bharata and Lakṣmaṇa’s younger brother remained in the city of their maternal uncle, Yudhājit. (1)
Then Daśaratha set his mind upon making his son Rāma—the Lord of the three worlds by his own nature—the sovereign over the mere territory of his own kingdom;
as if desirous of appointing that mountain of auspiciousness, who was capable of sustaining the burden of the universe, as the principal pillar for the roof-beams of his own palace-complex.
Immediately thereafter, having consulted with his ministers and having summoned the elders of the city, the aged Vṛddhaśravas, and the priests, he issued this command:

"It is indeed known to you that all our ancestors—maintaining a disposition solely toward auspiciousness, walking upon the excellent path, their minds compassionate toward living beings, rich in honor, ever-vigilant in the accumulation of fame, and intent on sweeping away the calamities of the people—having attained supreme bliss, have gone to the state of the gods."
Therefore, following their wisdom, we too have protected all subjects for this long duration. In this matter, you yourselves—who experience this act of protection by me—are indeed the authority.
Since the world certainly does not follow a path contrary to your accepted tenets and scriptures, there is truly nothing further to be requested.

Whether by my fame sung by gods and men, or by my weapons, or by my valor equal in its course throughout heaven and earth—old age, which is inevitably unavoidable, has appeared in my body like moonlight upon a cluster of blooming lotuses. (3)

Therefore, having been authorized by the noble ones, I desire to transfer upon this dear child—the burden of the earth that has been borne for a long time—and to enjoy the happiness of rest; for he is one who possesses a splendor of heroism more boundless than even the breaking of Bhārgava, whose terrifying appearance was due to his wielding the most excellent edge of the battle-axe that shatters the pride of the entire host of Kṣatriyas; he is a vessel of beauty, an abode of the people’s affection, free from envy, and full of compassion.

Then, like peacocks whose cries of joy flow forth unrestrainedly upon hearing the thundering of the massed rain-clouds of the monsoon, the people became resonant with the confused clamor of delight filling the quarters of the sky. A flood of tears of joy appeared on the faces of the subjects,
like nectar appearing upon a lotus, as if to wash their eyes with care so they might behold the splendor that Rama was destined to possess on the day of his consecration.

The King, too—his limbs covered in a profusion of horripilation as if desiring to ward off the falling columns of dust arising from the crush of people eager for the approaching great festival, and having attained a joy beyond measure—restrained within his heart an exultation redoubled by the intensity of his delight, and spoke thus to Sumanta and the other chief ministers:

"How can such devotion of the people arise toward Rāma, who has not yet departed for the regions of the penance groves where we have taken refuge, and who remains vigilant in protecting the path, while still clinging to his unfading innocence? (5)
They too, having restrained their own desires, addressed King Daśaratha with humility:
"O Lord, even while you remain, it is no wonder that people should of their own accord resort to your son Rāmabhadra;
for does a thirsty cakora bird go to the Ocean of Milk when there is the moon, which is the very cause of its finding [the nectar]? (6)

Immediately thereafter, at the command of Vasiṣṭha—the most eminent among the knowers of reality—the assembly of citizens, together with the ministers, set out to fetch the requisites for the consecration.
Summoning Rāma, who was charming in his humility, the Lord, manifesting his joy, spoke thus:
"On the day of Tiṣya, I shall strive to place the crown upon your noble head without delay. (7)
Then, having informed Kauśalyā of Daśaratha’s desire, the venerable Vasiṣṭha performed the auspicious rites of joy for Rāma, who had returned to his own residence.

Filling the quarters with the sounds of auspicious musical instruments, which acted like cymbals for the ears of the beloved ones who were eager for them, there arose an extraordinary and overflowing joy among the citizens and the country folk, beyond the reach of words. (8)
She whom they call the primary cause for the uprooting of the race of night-stalkers (demons), whose mind was naturally crooked and whose body became as it were a friend to her limbs;
like a female buffalo to the cool water of a lake, that Mantharā mercilessly churned the heart of Kaikeyī.

Alas, there was wickedness in Bharata’s mother toward the mother of Bharata [Kaikeyī], who— like a harsh thunderbolt amidst a mass of cool clouds due to the fault of being crushed by a violent, surging gale— had robbed the people of their happiness through her slow and treacherous words.

This very woman, her own mind possessed by the demoness named Mantharā, previously presented two boons to Daśaratha—who had been granted those boons by himself for the sake of dispelling the pain incurred during his battle with the Asura Śambara while residing in the city of Vaijayantī in Daṇḍaka.
Of these two, one was the intense agitation for the consecration of Bharata, and the other was the dwelling of Rāma in the forest, subsisting solely on wild fare. (11)

At that moment, the pair of earrings, having pierced the ears of the king—which were harsh from the pain of long-smelt copper arrows—filled his heart with the method of a sealed-vessel cooking (puṭapāka), for he was terrified of abandoning the truth. 12.
Then, from the heart of Daśaratha, whose mind was tormented by the mere news of his son’s separation,
consciousness departed like a doe suddenly fleeing from a deep cave as it is licked by the blazing flames of a forest fire.
Then Daśaratha, having somehow regained consciousness, spoke to Kaikeyī:
"Rāma will indeed depart for the forest, abandoning the long-held festivities; but how shall the world abandon the long-maintained festivities for his consecration?
Out of fear of the loss of dharma, I shall speak of the separation from my child; yet what more shall I say, O wife, until infamy, which produces suffering, arises for you as long as an eon? (14)

O hard-hearted Kaikeyī, my life surely cannot endure without Rāma, that delight to the eyes, who was like a calf to me; I believe that because the Creator has previously united him with you by his power, he now leads me to my own death.
Thereupon, Kaikeyī, intent on fulfilling her own single desire, spoke with derision:

"For you, who closely observe the violation of truth and the failure of your promise regarding your offspring, if there is indeed fruitlessness in what was promised, then here is this salutation with joined palms. (16)

O subduer of enemies, has he not come before your ears—he who is the foremost of those whose speech is truth, his limbs mangled by weapons for the sake of saving the life of a young pigeon that had become the prey of a hawk? (17)
Furthermore,
having worshipped and bestowed his own two eyes upon a certain Brahmin who had sought refuge with him,
a wise man named Alarka— whose power was renowned for fulfilling his vows— completely filled [the recipient’s sight]. (18)

Just as you, O Lord of Men, out of affection bestowed a pair of excellent garments upon me at the conclusion of the distress caused by the onset of the battle with the Asuras, so may those kings—who are true to their word and whose bonds of friendship are not loose—readily honor that promise with a "water-seal" (a formal oath). 19.
What is the use of much speaking?
Either speak words that are true here, or do not; I shall not tolerate the honor shown to Rāma’s mother on this earth.
If you do not abandon your ongoing preparation for battle, I shall remain here after consuming poison while you look on.
To her who spoke thus, the king spoke yet again:

"O hard-hearted one, why have you become devoid of compassion, having cast aside the moral laws of the world? You were not even counted among the virtuous women here, nor did that Rāma include you in the reckoning of those with fathers."
O ignoble woman, I shall not accept even the pleasures of my own sons, nor shall Bharata give me even water to drink. (21)
Furthermore,
let his clothing be the bark of trees, let the shade of forest trees be his palaces— blessed indeed—
and O Kaikeyī, how could even the hard stone slabs be beds for him, yet they seem harder than your own heart? (22)
Though thus rebuked by her husband, she did not become harsh-hearted, for her disposition was overcome by Mantharā;
she remained untroubled like a bed of moonstones shaded by creepers, even while the full moon shone upon it.
Thereafter, desiring to experience for even a mere moment the pleasure of beholding Rāma’s face, Daśaratha commanded Sumantra, "Bring the prince.

Quickly ushered into the royal palace by him, Rāma offered his salutations; then, observing his father’s countenance radiant with an unprecedented glow, he was struck with wonder and asked Kaikeyī, "What is this? That wicked-minded woman replied:

"My child, your father, though highly skilled in fulfilling the two boons he promised, now sinks deeply into a bottomless ocean of grief due to his affection for his son and his fear of violating the truth.
The two boons were: your dwelling in the forest according to the life of a sage, and the protection of the earth for Bharata.
Upon hearing this, Rāma, with a joyful heart, joined his palms in reverence and addressed her:
"O Mother, is Bharata, the bearer of the earth's burden, afraid? Or am I terrified of the purifying forest? And why does my father, the preeminent leader of Sagara’s lineage, grieve?
If they do not fulfill this light vow of ours by providing water for the divine river, how could she [the earth] ever become our daughter? (24)
In the forest land, I was commanded to protect my body alone, while the burden of the entire world was placed upon the head of my child.
Thus, when the relative ease of our respective tasks is considered, O Mother, your greater partiality falls upon me. (25)

Father, having personally proclaimed with his own voice the heart-warming auspiciousness of my consecration festival, was he not the worthy recipient of the full vessel (pūrṇapātra) offered by me as a sign of salutation? (26)

At that moment, like a mountain struck by lightning, like a great tree surrounded on all sides by a forest fire, and like Nahuṣa distressed by his fall from the station of the Lord of Heaven, Paṅktiratha fell down unconscious.
Then she commanded Rāma, "Carry out your father's instruction.
Bearing his mother’s command upon his head like a garland, the highly illustrious one [obeyed].
Rāma departed for the forest for the sake of protecting the worlds. ||27||
Having immediately reached the palace of Kausalyā, he reported to her—after first offering his salutations—the obstacle to the consecration, Kaikeyī’s obstinacy, and his own exile into the forest.
Upon hearing this, her heart rent asunder, she suddenly collapsed and lamented like one whose pair of ears had been pierced by arrows smeared with poison:
"O hand that brings welfare to the three worlds, marked with the lines of the chariot-wheel, the lotus, and the conch!"
The venerable Vasiṣṭha has surely performed the digging of a well in the wilderness and bound a protective amulet for you. ||28||
Thereupon, the son of Sumitrā, his wrath having increased excessively, spoke thus to his elder brother, who was equal to Indra:

"Noble brother, it is an improper act for you to abandon the kingdom and set out to wander the forest at the word of Kaikeyī—a woman deserving of the world's reproach—due to the King’s feebleness of intellect, which has rendered him mute regarding the distinction between what ought and ought not to be done, as his mind is overcome by passion, old age, and [the queen’s] influence. Moreover, the earth was indeed bestowed upon you by our father long ago, even before you had requested it."
Even the duty of a Kṣatriya, though it may deviate from the path of righteousness due to negligence in protecting the castes and stages of life, generally leads a person toward the supreme good.
Indeed, for a resolute man, human effort alone—by surely overcoming the power of destiny—accomplishes the goals of human existence.
Let there be no redness in your lotus-feet from wandering through the wilderness; let the redness of my palms spread slightly from the bowstring drawn back to my ear.
O noble ocean of valor, do not become submissive to the words of my father, who has been overpowered by Kaikeyī; let my bow remain ever bent. 29.
To Lakṣmaṇa, who was speaking thus, Rāma spoke while consoling him:
"My child, for those born of the Solar dynasty, the father’s command alone is the guide in all matters.

Indeed, many—such as Kaṇḍu, Raṇuka, Puru, and others—out of reverence for their father's command, have performed even the killing of a cow, the slaying of a mother, and the exchange of their youth; yet they are reckoned without hesitation as the foremost among the virtuous."
Therefore, it was certain that the father’s entry into the deep forest must indeed be undertaken.
Thereupon, Kausalyā, whose maternal affection for her son was vast, desiring to go along with him, was addressed with humility by Rāma, who had already offered his salutations:
"While I am dwelling in the wilderness, [the heart of] the daughter of the King of Kekaya has been shattered by my words, which have sprouted from the harshness of her nature."
O Mother, you must never neglect our father’s body, which is withered by the fire of grief.
Then she pronounced a blessing for her son’s well-being, preceded by the invocation of all the deities.
Thereafter, Rāma, having saluted her, departed; and as he left, he beheld the favor of Sītā, whose attire had been cast aside.
He suddenly defiled his beloved wife—who had been made happy by auspicious words—with the news of his wandering in the forest.
The Pulinda, as if terrifying the peahen in the forest who was delighted by the thundering of the clouds, with the sound of his bow. ||31||
He spoke to her as she set out to follow him:

"My dear daughter of Janaka, how can I bear to wither such a naturally graceful body of yours, as delicate as a *śirīṣa* flower, in this forest—the mouth of a wolf—where the faces of wild beasts are smeared with blood flowing from various wounds on the thighs of female deer they have seized? (32)

Thereafter, when Maithilī’s desire to follow him remained unawakened despite various efforts, and when Lakṣmaṇa too had not yet resolved upon the journey, he bestowed upon Vasiṣṭha’s son Suyajña all his ornaments along with a thousand elephants, including the intoxicated elephant named Śatruñjaya given by his maternal uncle; and he gave to Agastya and Kauśika highly precious jewels, as well as two bows capable of withstanding the power of the enemies of the gods, and two pieces of armor providing infallible protection.

Taking up this entire collection of weapons bestowed by Varuṇa at the assembly of the waters—weapons that were unattached, whose blades were rendered irresistible by limitless arrows, and which had been wielded by heroic hands—he urged the son of Sumitrā, saying, "Follow me.

Sītā, for her part, gave her own collection of ornaments to the wife of Suyajña. Then the son of Sumitrā also gratified a certain preceptor residing with Kausalyā with the wealth he had under his command.

There, the Lord of the Raghus bestowed upon the impoverished Brahmin named Trijaṭā, who had come with his family, a herd of cattle extending as far as the spot where his staff fell from his own hand; and he distributed various riches to Kapiñjala and other twice-born men.

Then, having drenched and scorched both the bodies and minds of the city women—whose bud-like lips trembled in the gale of their sighs and whose hearts were consumed by the fire of grief—with a downpour of tears, they departed from the inner apartments, their exile made manifest by the fact that they were forbidden from being followed by their attendants.

"Let Sītā, who was previously unseen even by those who travel through the sky, not become an object for the eyes of all mortal men"—having reflected thus, the Creator surely covered the eyes of embodied beings with the rising of tears. (33)
"Though she is confined, Maithilī follows me as I go; likewise, my dear Lakṣmaṇa never leaves me.
Having thus made them understand his intent to follow him, Rāma again entered the royal palace to depart.

When Sumantra had thus informed him and pointed out the way, the king, as if possessed by a spirit, fell from his seat along with his wife; and together with her, who was engaged in lamentation, he himself felt a longing for the forest.
Then Sumantra said to Kaikeyī:
"O Queen, desist from this obstinacy which obstructs the sprout of joy blossoming at the imminent consecration of Rāma."

Long ago, indeed, by virtue of a boon and grace, she had acquired the power of understanding the speech of all living beings. When the ants crawling along the edge of her father’s couch were conversing, she asked her father the reason for his laughter; having learned that the explanation was the cause of her husband’s death, she was disregarded by the king, who was incensed by her persistent importunity.

To ensure that her mother would not suffer the same fate, the daughter of Kekaya pointed to Sagara—who had brought about his own destruction through improper conduct—as an example, and thus restrained her husband.
The great minister Siddhārthaka spoke of abandoning that place because it was the cause of the death of many people who had fallen into the Sarayū River.
Then, though Daśaratha had instructed that Rāma should depart with all his attendants, he requested only a basket for digging and a pair of bark garments.
Kaikeyī brought the bark garments and other items for all three of them—those who were accustomed to comfort and possessed the manifest splendor of divine beauty. (37)
Then the lord of the Raghu clan, having lost hope regarding a virtuous and auspicious garment due to the command of his mother Kaikeyī,
donned a bark garment whose harshness was removed by the sprinkling of Jānaki’s tears as they glistened upon her swelling breasts.

There, everyone was struck with wonder as they beheld the leader of the Ikṣvāku clan, whose facial expression remained unchanged; for even upon the faces of those whose minds were pinned by the spikes of grief, no sign of emotion manifested in succession. When Vasiṣṭha closed his eyes out of despondency at the sight of Daśaratha’s son clad in bark garments, that very act became the instrument for the great sage’s perception of the true nature of Rāma’s lineage.
"Has there been some transformation in him that he has abandoned his yellow garment?
Thus, Vasiṣṭha, the best among those with inward vision, was not greatly distressed.

There, having embraced her daughter-in-law who was bowing down to depart for that journey, Kausalyā—her maternal affection for her son overflowing—became choked with tears.

As the scion of Raghu was about to begin his journey, Sītā mounted the chariot first.
Like the foremost light of the Lord of Days as he desires to mount his chariot, she ascended the chariot whose path was not blue.
And the two sons of Daśaratha ascended the chariot.
Just as Sītā became eager for the forest upon leaving the capital of the Raghava dynasty, so too did the royal fortune of the Rakshasa king become desirous of going to Laṅkā. (43)
"This city follows Rāmabhadra from its children to its elders; therefore, let us not indeed be devoid of merit here.
As if out of such devotion, the Earth, having assumed many forms under the guise of dust, followed after him. (44)
As his daughter was departing for the forest with her beloved husband— who had turned away from royal pleasures— due to the ripening of destiny,
the nurse, fearing it would be an ill omen, surely quickly covered the tears in the faces of the onlookers with dust.

With its crowds of citizens having departed in pursuit of the taste of following Rāma, and with its houses, courtyards, and royal highways reduced to mere structural shells, the capital of the bull among the Raghus became light in an instant, like the sloughed skin of a serpent that has cast off its coils. 46.

Then Daśaratha, together with the women of his inner apartments, departed from the city; and finding no other recourse, he gazed intently at that very Rāma, the delight of the Raghus, as he passed beyond the range of sight in the chariot driven by Sumantra. With a torrent of tears flowing forth, he fell to the ground, overcome by fainting.
Thereafter, having regained consciousness through the consolation offered by others, the king desired to go to the palace of Kaikeyī.

Then the son of Daśaratha, his chariot’s speed slackened by the difficulty of navigating through the surging mass of the great multitude who were pressing forward in a frantic scramble, reached the banks of the Tamasā.

There, as the people—whose minds were sinking in grief at the separation from the feet of the descendant of Kakutstha—resorted to the forest where cries of lamentation were manifest, the roots of the trees on the banks of the Tamasā became their houses, with their leafy beds spread upon the ground. (47)

Then, at midnight, the son of Daśaratha, having consulted with Sumantra and deceived the crowds of people, set out in a chariot that bowed low under its burden and reached the foot of an *iṅgudī* tree—the ornament of Śṛṅgaverapura—which was embraced by the celestial Gaṅgā at its peak and stood at the root of a tree where the waves of the Gaṅgā touched it; he passed beyond the earth given to Ikṣvāku by Manu, which was adorned by the three rivers flowing from the ears of Vasiṣṭha’s cow, following a path where the tracks of the chariot and the hoofprints of the horses were hidden by various forest thickets, creepers, and layers of grass.

Having beheld Rāma—who was visible due to auspicious deeds accumulated over many births—and having heard from his two mothers the account of his life as a forest-dweller, the lord of the Niṣādas, his face covered by incessant tears born of intensely surging joy and grief, became drenched with those drops possessing the quality of coldness. (48)
Having approached his dear friend Guha, Raghunātha was immediately entreated by him with palms joined in reverence:
"O Lord, although your heart is inclined toward the command of your father, these words—born of the common usage of the ignorant—compel me to speak.

Indeed, this kingdom of ours is possessed of a multitude of fortresses guarded by soldiers formidable in their irresistible prowess; it is filled with an abundance of enjoyments and is slow to yield, causing pain even to the heart of Mantharā."

"Having accepted this person—who has been engaged in tasks since time immemorial—and having favored him somewhat as one worthy of his attendants and a vessel of fortune, may you, without abandoning this man, complete the fourteen years mentioned by Daśaratha in this land of wondrous power, amidst the assembly of sages, so that the painful sight of separation from your mother may be mitigated by the vision of the Mandākinī.
To her friend who thus made this request, Rāmabhadra replied with kind words:
