Then, in accordance with that [the king's] request, while a breeze from the river’s waves blew very gently—carrying a mass of honey-drops dripping from clusters of lotuses that were being crushed by the chariots controlled by Sumantra—the two sons of Daśaratha offered hospitality with the traditional *madhuparka* beneath a tree on the bank; and when the final twilight, the presiding deity of the day, had vanished behind the western mountain as if unable to bear the sight of their departure for the forest, Rāma completed his evening rites and took up his place upon a bed of leaves prepared by Lakṣmaṇa at the foot of that tree.
As Rāma entered the inner apartment known as Tarumūla with the daughter of Videha, attended by Lakṣmaṇa as his chamberlain,
the Lord of the Niṣādas, having observed him and restrained his boundless torrent of tears, cast off sleep and sat down.

When the night had passed, at the peak of the eastern mountain which was stealing the garland of rays from the sun, the two sons of Daśaratha, having bound their matted locks, went together with Sītā to the banks of the Bhāgīrathī.
There, Rāma, his heart filled with joy, spoke to Sītā:
"Of the great fever caused by the wrath of Kapila, which arose from the search for the path of the sacrificial horse, [you are the divine medicine]."
We take refuge in the blessed Bhāgīrathī, whose fortune has reached its full maturity through the propitiation of her father. ||51||
Immediately thereafter, Rāma—having had Sumantra turned back by his gentle words—ascended the boat brought by Guha along with Maithilī, who was entreating him.

Having forbidden even the lord of the Niṣādas from following them, he quickly crossed over to the opposite bank of the celestial river and set foot in the land called Vatsa, where the crops were fully ripened. There, having slain four deer that were skilled in piercing targets, he spent the night at the foot of a certain tree.

On the following day, traveling by a forest path, they reached the hermitage of Bhāradvāja at Prayāga, where the mass of smoke from spreading sacrificial oblations was rising; having paid their respects to that great sage with boundless joy, and being directed by him along the prescribed route, they crossed the flood of the Vaikartanī river by means of a bamboo raft. Then they reached Mount Citrakūṭa, which was variegated by the conduct of all beings who had abandoned the pride of their learning through the proximity of people whose hearts were full of tranquility. There, they dwelt in delightful leaf-huts constructed by their younger brother, which were graced by the fifth notes trilling from the throats of intoxicated cuckoos.
Through his union with the daughter of Janaka, Rāma experienced the happiness of Sāketa and rejoiced for a long time upon the plateaus of Citrakūṭa.

Then Sumantra, dependent upon the hope that Rāma might still summon him out of a desire for forest-dwelling, spent several days in the presence of Guha; but losing all hope, he returned thence and reached Ayodhyā, where festivities had ceased. Alighting from his chariot amidst the wailing of the citizens, who were blinded by the excess of their grief at the news that he had arrived without the two sons of Daśaratha, he prostrated himself before Daśaratha, whose life-breaths were on the verge of departing as he prepared for his final journey.

Upon seeing this, Daśaratha fell unconscious; he was revived by Kausalyā and Sumitrā, and with his throat choked with tears, he questioned Sumantra again and again: "How did Rāma depart? How did Maithilī? What was the condition of the son of Sumitrā?
He, in turn, informed the king:
"O King, how can I speak? I am hard-hearted."
Your two sons, who had long been the objects of the citizens' desires following their devotion to service, and who were far removed from your chariot,
became the new attendants of the daughter of Videha and turned into travelers in the forest on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī.
O King, at the time of your son’s coronation, even the husband of Arundhatī was not able to sprinkle the mass of his locks with milk produced from his own cows;
alas, he has now been sprinkled with the tears shed by the Maithila princesses—tears that serve as milk brought by the Niṣādas to form his matted locks.
On the toenails of that daughter of Videha, a redness appeared instantly even without lac;
yet as she walked along the forest path with her beloved, no pallor ever manifested upon her face.

Having prepared a bed for the Lord of Sītā with the young shoots [of trees] and having directed his gaze toward the subduing of the demons during the nights, Lakṣmaṇa, the archer, remained sleepless on the forest path as if out of devotion to His feet—a state attainable through merit alone. (56)

Thus, having been informed of his son’s conduct by Sumantra, and having consoled Sauśalyā—who bore the arrow of grief fixed in her heart—as she sat upon the peak of the western mountain while the sun, whose form is the Vedas, was setting, the king spoke as follows:
"In former times, indeed, on the banks of the Sarayū, where the lord of heaven was concealed by a multitude of various trees, I spent a certain period of time out of a desire for the hunt.
There—"
While crossing the Sarayū river, I—a knower of the art of hitting a target by sound—pierced a certain ascetic who was carrying water, mistaking him for an elephant trumpeting in a lotus pond.
As he was about to ascend the funeral pyre of his aged and blind parents to follow them in death, a curse fell upon you: "May even you perish through love for your son. (57)
"I was born to a Vaiśya father from a Śūdra mother; therefore, it could not have happened.
Having told me, 'It is the killing of a Brāhmaṇa,' the distressed sage departed for heaven. (58)
"Therefore, I am certainly subject to death"—with this thought crossing his mind, Rāma himself ceased speaking. Misfortune, brought about by the sage’s curse, is beyond remedy;
thus, it swiftly reduced Daśaratha to his tenth stage [death]. (59)

Although he did not allow heaven to be invaded by enemies, nor did he permit the beloved wives of the gods to be taken captive, nor did he fill the outer courtyard of Sāketa with the messengers of Indra;
and although he did not command his ministers for the protection of the earth, yet Daśaratha went to the celestial realm out of grief, unable to endure staying in his vehicle.

Then, as the quarters of the sky resounded with the lamentations of the women of Avarādha— intensified by the praises of Daśaratha, sprouting from the censures of Kaikeyī, and multiplied by the chanting of Rāma’s virtues—
the courtyard of the sky became devoid of its noble stars due to the absence of a king;
and as if observing that, the entire surface of the earth was instantly stilled.

Then at dawn, acting upon the word of Vasiṣṭha, the ministers placed the king’s body in a vat of oil and dispatched messengers to the Kekayas with the command: "Bring Bharata here immediately, without mentioning anything of Daśaratha's fate.

They too, traveling on a path shortened by horses as swift as the wind, arrived at the city of the Lord of Horses and saluted Bharata, whose mind was troubled by an ominous dream, and informed him of their master’s command.
Having received permission from his maternal grandfather Yudhājit, he set out; after only a few days, filled with apprehension due to the occurrence of ill omens, he reached Sāketa.
With a mind filled with great apprehension, seeing the city already before him with its citizens moving about in an unprecedented manner,
Bharata, accompanied by his messengers, entered the royal palace from the ancestral grove, which was no less than a cemetery.

Without looking back at his father, he went to his mother’s dwelling; having prostrated before her, he asked, "Where indeed has my father gone? To Bharata, she spoke these exceedingly harsh words: (63)
Like a forest-dweller, Rāmabhadra set out together with the princess of Mithilā and Lakṣmaṇa to fulfill his father’s final rites;
thereafter, your father succumbed to the law of time, so may you enjoy the earth as you wish, free from all rivals.
Like a peahen with her cry to a great serpent, the daughter of Kekaya,
by means of her speech, made Bharata’s mind deeply agitated.
Thereupon, having lamented for a very long time, Bharata—his humanity and discernment utterly lost—spoke to Kaikeyī:

"You are not our mother, for you are the convergence of four evils that have become harsh in their final outcome. Therefore, let the mothers of sons speak as they please; but infamy shall call you 'mother' when it reaches the ears of those who suffer. (66)
Thereupon, his gaze drawn toward her face, he spoke this to his younger brother:

"Alas! While you, O Satī, remain present—scattering heat upon the hearts of people to consume them with an unceasing and fresh lineage of suffering—how can the Goddess, who is worshipped by the sinless at every moment, now bear the name 'Āśrayāśā' (the Consumer of Her Refuge)?"
Even for a cow, upon seeing her calf whose grazing has not yet ceased, tears flow from the eyes of all the hundred deer who are its companions;
tell me, then, how can the daughter of the Lord of Kosala now cross over this grief for her son, she who has but one child? (68)
Moreover, O King, by the conjunction of time and through the two excellent arrows of this mantra, the vital breath of that [enemy] was led away;
his departure from the city to dwell somewhere on the ground of a cemetery amidst anthills is indeed most fitting.

Alas, how did this woman of base intellect appear in the Kekaya lineage—a family that has produced many noble scions worthy of themselves—like a poisonous creeper in a forest abounding with mango trees? (70)

"Though I am bereft of my mother," that hero, a knower of dharma, thought, "I have my mother"—just as one who has escaped from one hell to another might think, "I have escaped from hell," so did he feel with his younger brother. (71)

There, Kausalyā, accompanied by her ministers, approached and desired to ascend the funeral pyre of her husband; but Bharata, having restrained her with hundreds of oaths, performed the funeral rites as intended by the sacrificers at Yāgaśilā, following the path ordained by Vasiṣṭha.

When his father had gone to the forest of the ancestors (the cremation ground), the skillful Bharata, with palms joined in reverence, likewise requested the subjects to go to the forest of his brothers.
Then, entreated by Sumitrā, Kausalyā, and the women of the inner apartments, Bharata returned to his residence.

Thereupon, after the funeral rites had been performed according to the rules and fourteen days had passed, the ministers, accompanied by the family priest—who was well-disposed toward the solar dynasty—and the city elders, approached him and requested that he wear the crown.
To those who were thus pressing him, he replied:
What is the use of many words spoken here? Having abandoned the conduct of Saumitri, I shall bear even the crown, for your command is venerable.
If there is not even a single place in the vast Daṇḍaka forest suitable for my leaf-hut, then I have no other recourse.
Having spoken thus, her mind eager for service to Śrī Rāma, she departed.

Having prepared a deceptive path and having created dustiness upon the virtuous way—which is adverse to the pleasure of the eyes of the good—there arose from the midst of the king’s palace a whirlwind named Mantharā, moving swiftly with a crooked course. (74)
Seizing by her own hand the mass of hair of that younger brother of Rāma who was intent on killing him, Kausalyā restrained the enraged man. (75)

Thereupon, having departed from the city with his inner apartments, Bharata followed a path prepared by a multitude of artisans. As he proceeded, he caused the celestial Gaṅgā to tremble with the mass of dust raised from the surface of the earth, which was trampled by the feet of the men, elephants, chariots, and horses spread out before him. With the consent of Guha, who was moved by the multitude of virtues recounted by Sumantra, he crossed the river and, having deposited his load of bark garments at the gate of the hermitage of Dīrghatapas, paid homage to Bharadvāja.
With a joyful mind, the sage Bharadvāja beheld Bharata and each member of his mother’s kin, and having summoned the army as well, he offered them hospitality as was appropriate.
In that same manner, Bharadvāja—whose every deity was like a warrior upon his brow—extended hospitality to those embodied beings who were dear to Bharata;
for they, having performed severe penance and now enjoying the fruits thereof in heaven, would desire even for a moment the satisfaction bestowed by the sage, just as celestial flowers do.
Thus, having spent that day—which felt like a hundred days—there according to the sage’s instruction, they all entered the region of the Citrakūṭa forest.

Having left the army there, Guha searched for Rāma here and there; and from afar, he perceived him by the mountain breeze fragrant with the scent of oblations and the smell of smoke, by the mountain herds of deer, and by the vicinity where the sound of Lakṣmaṇa’s bow was heard—a sound appropriate for the expulsion of flesh-eating Piśācas and which served as a mantra for scattering the offerings of flowers by the forest deities whose forms were invisible.

The region was crowded with the families of Vāikhānasa sages dwelling in newly constructed leaf-huts, wearing bark garments and deerskins hanging from the branches of forest trees; it was thick with dense showers released from the sprout-like hands of the hosts of celestial armies, gathered from the branches of the divine trees and variegated by fragments of fresh foliage.

Bharata hurriedly approached Rāma’s hermitage—a place that rivaled the splendor of Sāketa; where the pedestal at the foot of the tree where Jānakī resided was being worshipped with heaps of flowers; where swords, bows, and quivers were visible; where one portion was prepared with roots, tubers, and fruits gathered by the son of Sumitrā who was ever-anxious for guests; and which, through the presence of Janaka’s daughter whose lotus-feet were never absent from there, mocked the beauty of the city of Ayodhyā.

Then he beheld the lotus-eyed one, clad in bark garments, dark as a fresh rain-cloud, who had made his abode in that place difficult even for the virtuous to attain, yet which was the very source of peace.
He beheld the glorious one, his matted locks bound up, his arms resembling the coils of the lord of serpents, accompanied by Sītā upon the forest ground. (77)
Then, near him, she paid homage to Vaidehī, whose birth was dependent upon Janaka and Yajñadatta, who was like a fresh crescent of the moon;
she who, through the familiarity of the impressions of her lotus feet arising from the merit of the great forests, maintained in its entirety the auspicious state of the city of Ayodhyā.
He in whom the title "Rāmānuja"—difficult for others to attain—is self-evidently victorious in this world even over the status of being the son of Sumitrā;
he who, had the pair of lotuses been a mere reflection of his own eyes, would have rendered them truly sleepless in the darkness of the night. (79)

Immediately thereafter, on a desert path in the height of summer, he—having by chance discovered a lotus pond whose waters were filled with nectar—approached it with haste like a thirsty black antelope scorched by intense heat. Falling at the feet of Rāma, who was accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, he wept for a long time and related the story of Daśaratha, thereby inducing a swoon of grief in Rāma. While these [sages] were causing the ocean of sorrow to overflow its shores, the self-knowing Vasiṣṭha acted as Agastya toward that very ocean. (80)
Then, having received the teacher’s permission and performed the appropriate rites of bathing in the river of the immortals, Bharata prostrated before Rāma and set out to bring him back.

Manifesting an intention that was favorable to the lineage of the Sun, consistent with his multitude of virtues, worthy of his fame and form, suitable to his conduct, befitting his ancestral fortune, undeserving of public reproach, and in harmony with his learning—such was the petition initiated by Bharata.

At that moment, having respectfully prostrated before me—my head marked by the touch of royal fortune which is as fragile as a flash of lightning, and now cast down by hundreds of kings—he made this request himself: "May you two adorn my sandals. Then, as if to proclaim his own status, Bharata placed his head upon my feet, which were like those of one who sleeps upon the bare ground.
But Rāma rejected even these words with another speech: "The duty toward our father, whose word is truth, must be performed by you and by me alike. (81)
There, even though Jābāli’s entreaty was in vain,

Bharata, the best among those who know how to gain what is beneficial, subsequently made his request and obtained two highly precious crowns fashioned in the form of the sandals of the descendant of Kakutstha. (82)
By his brother's command, he set out for Ayodhyā along with his younger brothers;
meanwhile, Rāma went to the forest with Lakṣmaṇa in accordance with his father’s instruction.
Having traversed various countries, Bharata, clad in bark garments,
reached his own territory and turned his back upon that realm.

Then he resolved: "Until the noble one’s return, I shall not dwell in Ayodhyā; if he exceeds that limit and delays, I shall immediately resort to fire and delight my life-breaths. With this thought, he took refuge in a hermitage known as Nandigrāma.
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, also entered the depths of the dense forest to avoid the slaughter wrought by the hosts of night-stalkers described by the sage Śamadhanaja.
He was watched longingly by the forest deer with wide eyes—creatures whose growth was free from fear, yet who had lost all relish even for grazing upon the darbha grass.
Having reached the abode of the great seer Atri, which is honored by all beings, Rāma, his mind filled with joy, accepted the worship offered by him with overflowing affection.
His wife, named Anasūyā, gratified Sītā with her own ornaments.
Then Rāghava reached the Daṇḍaka forest, like the fierce-rayed sun reaching the mass of clouds, in order to shatter the minds of his enemies—which were like white lotuses—to the earth-bride. (86)

Then Hanumān, possessing the speed of the king of birds and endowed with preeminent velocity, rose from a plateau of Mount Mahendra to search for Sītā, who had been carried away by the Ten-necked One, along the path of the celestial bards.

At that time, this mountain—unable to endure the crushing pressure of his feet firmly planted during the crossing of the ocean—seemed as if shedding a continuous rain of tears through its cascading torrents of water; with its masses of clouds spread here and there, it appeared like one whose braided hair was disheveled and flowing; and with the herds of elephants in a state of panic, it seemed as if it had developed a swelling.

It appeared as if its blood were flowing because its rugged ridges were reddened by the mass of mineral dust raised by the splitting of the ground from the tips of the exceedingly sharp hooves of herds of deer fleeing in terror; it seemed to have let out a cry because its caves were made resonant by lions awakened at that moment; it looked as if its garland of entrails had spilled out because of the snakes emerging from the dense thickets of the surrounding hollows; and it appeared to be covered in sweat because its form was bristling with the spray of water droplets falling from the masses of clouds struck by the tips of the branches of swaying trees.

With the sky filled by the whistling of the wind as it swelled within the hollows of bamboo stalks shattered by the falling of crystal boulders, he experienced a distress beyond the reach of words, like one whose upward breath is increasing. Then, following in its wake with a speed born from leaping over the path of the Wind-god, a multitude of trees from the thickets of Mount Mahendra fell in succession. In the midst of the ocean, they created the illusion of a multitude of stakes driven into the sea for the foundation lines of the future bridge, as their branches displayed their tops above the water.

The mountain Maināka emerged in great agitation from the ocean—whose rows of waves were driven by the force of the impact of his wings—to provide a place of rest for the son of the Wind-god; its lofty peaks pierced the realm of heaven.
There, seeing that an obstacle to his journey had arisen, Hiraṇyanābha, having cast him down with his chest and consoling him as he was departing, said:
"O gentle one, I have been impelled today by the grateful Sāgara to relieve your fatigue from the road; rest and then proceed."
Formerly, I was protected by your father from the one who splits mountains; therefore, I am not an adversary today, but rather an ally—so accept me.
When Hanumān had thus honored him who was making this request and departed according to the requirements of the task, [the Lord spoke].

Beholding Hiraṇyanābha turning back from the ocean with his forces, Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, whose hundredfold wrath had been aroused by the pride of his power, became free from anger toward him because of his service to the son of Pavamāna.

Thereafter, as Hanumān was rushing toward the city of Laṅkā just as before, Surasā—the mother of the double-tongued serpents—obstructed his path with her gaping mouth, like the Vindhya mountain blocking the course of the Sun’s charioteer.

As the son of the Wind-god swiftly expanded his form to overcome Surasā, his feet became immersed in the ocean; meanwhile, his head bore a garland of spray scattered by the mass of waves from the celestial river Gaṅgā.
Then Hanumān, having made his body slender and having entered that belly, emerged from it and performed the very stride of Trivikrama, the wielder of the discus.

Furthermore, as he proceeded on his way, this very messenger of Raghunātha—possessing the speed of a man-lion—cut through the body of Siṃhikā with his sharp hooves, his anger aroused by her obstruction of the shadow.

Thereafter, hanging from a towering peak on the far shore of the ocean, his body becoming exceedingly slender, he reached the northern gate-tower of the city of Laṅkā and became one whose inner heart was woven with threads of intense anxiety.

"How shall the monkey army cross this ocean that spreads such an obstacle? How indeed can it reach this capital city of the Yātudhānas? In every way, the son of Daśaratha’s hopes are frustrated; the leaping of the ocean has been rendered futile, and I alone have remained [as a witness]. I do not even know whether Jānakī still lives or not. Desiring thus to approach the venerable Sītā there, the son of Añjanā, for the sake of moving about in concealment, longed solely for the setting of the sun, the garlanded with rays.

Thereafter, as the divine sun entered the western quarter—as if to inform Varuṇa that the time for his purpose was drawing near, now that he had laid aside his bow in the presence of Agastya, who had performed a hundred sacrifices—;

Is this sky reddened by the rows of flame-tips from forest fires arising in the wilds and mountain valleys of distant lands? When the twilight glow had arisen, engendering a multitude of doubts in all people as to whether it was the mass of flames from the submarine fire of the final ocean that had stirred itself up to taste even the waters of the celestial river in the sky, or something else; when the bees—the twice-born—were wandering for alms of nectar from every lotus-palace, their leaf-cupped temples closed like lids; and when the evening breezes were rendered turbid by dragging at the buds of blooming blue water-lilies, here and there...

While the darkness spread abroad; while the gateways of the cities of the world-protectors were blackened by dense clouds of incense from black aloe-wood; while the plaintive cries of the cakravāka birds—the very prologue to the agony of separation—resounded across every lotus pond; and while the elephant of the sky was adorned with a garland of stars, there appeared upon the peak of the eastern mountain the moon, the life-breath of passion and the axe that fells the dark forest of tamāla trees.
Those who committed that act, obstructed by darkness, shone in the courtyard of the sky like sprouts of lotus-stalks covered by a mass of moss in a lake. ||11||

At that hour of twilight, Hanumān suddenly appeared, removing the curtain of the enemy's fame, like a stage director for the new drama of his entry into Laṅkā, in order to delight the minds of the virtuous. 12.

At that time, having defeated the presiding deity of Laṅkā—who had assumed the form of a young woman to obstruct his path and was threatening him repeatedly—and having received her consent after she informed him, by the command of the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā), of the destruction of her own abode caused by the insult initiated by the monkey, the Wind-god’s son (Hanumān) searched thoroughly for Maithilī in Laṅkā and reached the palace of the sovereign of the Nairṛtas.

Having devastated the multitude of trees in the Aśoka grove and experiencing only the entanglement of the spider-silk threads of the Rākṣasas out of curiosity to see you, we have approached your presence.
